Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2 
CRU International Limited confidential 
Executive summary 
Gold: nearing its peak 
After two years of rapid expansion, the gold market surplus dropped to 1,138 tonnes in 2011.  
This is 21% lower than in 2010, and reflects increased purchases by the official sector and lower 
scrap supplies alongside a fabrication demand that was largely flat. 
 Although gold has delivered no growth in price terms during the first half of 2012, we expect 
prices to resume their upward trend in the next six months. However, we believe that the 
gains for the year as a whole are likely to be moderate.  Overall, we forecast that the gold 
price will average $1,680/oz in 2012. 
 In 2013, we expect gold’s price rally to falter largely because of investors re-evaluating the 
risks that global financial markets face as well as higher levels of investor fatigue.  In the 
years beyond 2013, a sustained rise in interest rates and improvement in global economic 
conditions could prompt investors to intensify liquidation of their long positions in gold.  
The average gold price over our forecast period is expected to equal $1,603/oz in nominal 
terms and $1,542/oz in real terms as quotations continue to slip year-on-year to at least 2016. 
 Mine supply is expected to grow steadily throughout our whole outlook period.  However, in 
an environment of declining prices, the importance of producer hedging could increase. 
 Over the next five years, global gold supply may increase by a net 5% with steady growth 
witnessed in the 2012-15 period.  In the final year of our outlook, we expect growth to give 
way to contraction, perhaps of 1.5%, largely because of a sizeable drop in secondary supplies 
as they respond to lower gold prices. 
 We expect total fabrication demand for gold to get close to its pre-crisis 2007 level by 2016.  
However, it may need another year or two before the recovery from the effects of the global 
financial crisis is entirely complete. 
 India and China will remain the world’s two largest markets for gold jewellery for at least 
another five years.  However, both countries could struggle to maintain their past furious 
growth over the period.  China is likely to overtake India in 2012 and become the largest 
gold jewellery market over a full calendar year for the first time.  But India may reclaim its 
status of the world’s largest gold jewellery market in 2016 when China’s gold jewellery 
market may experience its first fall in a number of years. 
 Gold fabrication for other applications is unlikely to demonstrate growth this year given the 
tough economic climate many countries have been facing so far.  The pressure may start to 
ease in 2013, when we expect gold prices to begin to move lower.

Other precious metal markets 
 
Silver 
Weakening economic growth has continued to curtail industrial demand for silver.  Silver’s 
price has therefore not been immune to the wider sell-off among the base metals and has shed 
about 15% of its US dollar value during the last three months.  Its fortunes were clearly marked 
out from gold by the gold:silver price ratio rising from 51-52 to 58-59. 
 Fabrication demand in 2011 slowed more markedly than we previously thought.  Indeed, we 
now have it slipping by 1-1.5%.  And from a lower base, we now have offtake taking a 
slower path so that the total is 900 tonnes lower in 2016 than we were quoting last time. 
 The cut to our estimate of mine production in 2011 is minor and we continue to forecast it 
rising to 27,000 tonnes in 2016.  This assumes that delays to financing slow project develop-
ment and that silver’s price fallen by the time that such funding is easier to come by. 
 We continue to believe investor buying will continue to support silver’s price until 2014 and 
this should prevent project development from rising unchecked.  Nevertheless, weaker 
fabrication demand could now leave the global surplus running at 5,000 t/y through to 2016. 
 
Platinum 
We still expect platinum’s fundamental surplus to narrow in 2012.  However, its size in 
absolute terms will be slightly higher than we envisioned in March.  The shift of the market into 
deficit is now expected only in 2015. 
 Platinum mine output is likely to be lower this year than previously expected largely because 
of the rising likelihood that supplies from South Africa will post another annual decline. 
 Anticipated weakness in demand from the global glass industry together with constantly 
increasing volumes of scrap metal may undercut total net fabrication demand in 2012.  
 
Palladium 
As in our March forecast, we expect the palladium market to remain oversupplied in 2012 on 
both the fundamental and final levels. If shipments from Russian state stocks halt in 2014, as 
expected, the market may then swing back into a deficit on both levels. 
 Net demand is likely to take another little retracement this year before it resumes its upward 
trend.  Another surge in supplies of metal recovered from end-of-life vehicles, albeit of a 
smaller size than in 2011, should outweigh the moderate growth in underlying fabrication 
demand in 2012.  Increased scrap availability is meanwhile boosting this year’s supply. 
 The decline in primary production of palladium is likely to be steeper in 2012 than we 
anticipated in March.  Alongside our expectations of lower output from South Africa, we 
have downgraded our production estimates for Russian and North American palladium 
miners.

Data sources and study team 
The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of 
sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial 
Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of 
Metal Statistics (WBMS), CPM, GTIS trade statistics, company websites and written reports. 
 
However, CRU’s interpretation of the data may or may not coincide with those expressed in 
these various sources. 
 
The forecast is exclusively CRU’s. 
 
This report is based on information available to CRU up until 22nd June 2012.
